A pail is a container used for holding and carrying things — most often liquids like water or milk, but also loose materials like sand or paint. It is open at the top, has a flat bottom, and almost always has a handle attached to its rim so you can carry it easily.

In plain terms: if you picture a child at the beach scooping up sand, or a farmer carrying milk from a cow, or someone mopping a floor — the container they're using is a pail.

A pail is typically:

  • Cylindrical or slightly cone-shaped — wider at the top than at the bottom, or the same width all the way down.
  • Open at the top — there is no lid in its basic form (though some pails do come with lids).
  • Equipped with a handle — usually a curved, arching handle (sometimes called a "bail") fixed to opposite sides of the rim. This is what lets you swing it or carry it in your hand.
  • Relatively sturdy — built to hold weight without bending or breaking.

Pails can be made from different materials depending on their purpose:

  • Plastic — the most common today; lightweight, colorful, and inexpensive.
  • Metal (galvanized steel or tin) — traditional and durable; often used on farms or in industrial settings.
  • Wood — old-fashioned; historically used before plastic and metal became widespread.

Pails are workhorses. They show up in many everyday situations:

  • Carrying water — to water plants, clean a floor, or fill a trough for animals.
  • Milking — farmers collect milk from cows directly into a pail.
  • Cleaning — a mop bucket is essentially a large pail.
  • Painting — painters pour paint into a pail for easy access.
  • Playing — children use small colorful pails (often called sand pails) to scoop and mold sand at the beach or in a sandbox.
  • Storing things — nuts, bolts, berries, feed for animals — a pail can hold almost anything.
  • Firefighting (historically) — before fire trucks, people would pass pails of water down a line to douse fires.

A pail does not have one fixed size, but it generally holds somewhere between 1 and 5 gallons (roughly 4 to 20 liters). The word is used for containers in this practical, hand-carry range — not giant tanks, and not tiny cups.

You will also commonly see "a pail of something" used as a unit of measure:

  • "She fetched a pail of water from the well."
  • "He mixed a pail of cement."
  • "They picked a whole pail of blueberries."

This phrasing means the pail is full, or at least substantially filled, with that thing.
Pail vs. Bucket — Are They the Same?

This is a fair question, because the two words are used almost interchangeably in everyday speech, and for good reason: they refer to essentially the same object.

Both are open-topped, handled containers for carrying things. The difference, where one exists, is mostly about context and region:

  • "Pail" tends to appear in more traditional, rural, or specific contexts — a milk pail, a sand pail, a coal pail. It has a slightly old-fashioned or country feel.
  • "Bucket" is the more common, everyday word in modern American English — kick the bucket, bucket list, bucket of fried chicken.
  • In some regions (parts of the American Northeast and Canada), people naturally say "pail" where others would say "bucket."
  • In British English, "bucket" is heavily preferred.

So if you hear or read "pail," simply picture a bucket. You will not be wrong.

• The well was deep, and she lowered the pail on a rope to reach the water.
  • He left a pail under the leaking pipe to catch the drips.
  • The toddler proudly carried a little red pail to fill with seashells.
  • Three pails of water weren't enough to put out the flames.
  • The painter rinsed his brushes in a pail of soapy water.
A pail is a sturdy, open-topped container with a handle, used for carrying or holding liquids or loose materials — essentially what most people call a bucket.
